evidence_loop.label: the verdicts that never left the run — a proof that could no longer be attached, findings the exit code never carried
evidence_loop.summary: One runtime release, two changes on the same fault line: a diagnosis existed inside a run and nothing carried it out. `runtime:bootstrap plan` accepted a proof opt-in set that its own terminalization rule would later make unextendable, and said nothing at the only moment the operator could still act — the run completes and terminalizes the instant every required proof passes, so a proof not opted into at plan time can never be attached afterwards. `runtime:doctor` reported findings in its text and JSON and then exited 0 regardless, so no caller, script or CI step could act on a verdict the run had already reached. The release replaces the single exit code with a diagnostic ladder, which is a breaking change to every caller that read 0 as `nothing to see`; `record-failed` takes precedence at 40 and hides lower findings, so `overall.status` stays part of the verdict.

feature_commits.note: The exit-code ladder. BREAKING: doctor previously exited 0 whatever it found. `record-failed` sits first at 40 and by design HIDES any finding under it, so callers must read `overall.status` too: a caller must fail closed when no artifact exists rather than import a record whose hash points nowhere.

The plan-time warning. The failure it closes is not a crash: the run does exactly what it was asked, completes, terminalizes, and the omission only becomes visible later, when the proof can no longer be attached and the only recovery is a fresh plan and a full re-execution.

install_method: Not performed by this recovery. Both hosts already served 0.95.0 when it began — Claude's cache holds 0.93.0, 0.94.0 and 0.95.0 side by side with superseded trees marked `.orphaned_at`, Codex's holds 0.95.0 alone — so what is attested is a verification, not an install. Verbs remain host-specific as recorded in the preceding loops.
narrative:
Both changes in this release are the same bug wearing different clothes: a run reaches a verdict and has no way to hand it to whoever needed it.

The doctor half is the plainer one. Doctor has always reported findings — in its text output, in its JSON, in the artifact it records — and has always exited 0. Every non-interactive consumer of it was therefore reading a constant. The ladder gives the code a meaning, and the ordering of the ladder is the part that had to be argued rather than chosen: a `--record` failure sits at 40 and is explicitly documented as hiding whatever findings sit underneath it, so the command tells its reader to consult `overall.status` too. A ladder that let one failure mask another would have reproduced the original defect one level up. It is a breaking change, and it is typed as one, because a caller that read 0 as `nothing to see` will now see a non-zero code on a run that has not changed its behaviour at all.

The bootstrap half is quieter and, for the operator, worse. `runtime:bootstrap` terminalizes a run the moment every required proof has passed. That is correct on its own terms — there is nothing left to wait for. The consequence is that the set of proofs is fixed at plan time and cannot be widened afterwards: a proof not opted into then can never be attached, and the only recovery is a fresh plan and a full re-execution of everything that already passed. Nothing said so at plan time, which is the only moment the operator could still act on it. The change adds the warning there. It closes no crash and fixes no wrong answer; what it repairs is the gap between when a decision becomes irreversible and when the tool admits it.

The recovery itself surfaced one thing worth recording, and it is a lesson about measurement rather than about either change. The scorecard has carried a whole-tree digest of the installed package for several loops, presented as the evidence that the two hosts hold identical bytes. This recovery first concluded that the number was unreproducible: five candidate recipes were run against the 0.94.0 cache, whose digest is published, and none matched. That conclusion was wrong, and the cross-host review disproved it. Every one of the five candidates used shasum's own hash-first output format; the original recipe emits the path first. Run in that form it reproduces 9b66e6de… exactly. What is actually wrong with it is narrower and worth fixing: it lives in a session transcript rather than in any repository script, and it is ambient-locale dependent — the same listing sorted under LC_ALL=C hashes to something else entirely. So the recipe is now written down, locale included, and the digest published here is taken under it and stays comparable with every record before this one. Replacing it with a new incomparable number, which is what this recovery first proposed, would have destroyed that continuity to solve a problem that did not exist.

The byte comparison itself also had to be re-taken. It was first run against ~/.codex/plugins/cache, an auxiliary tree; Codex actually serves runtime from the marketplace checkout that `codex plugin list --json` reports. The conclusion held either way, but a measurement that happens to be true is not the same as one that was taken correctly.
